note: Named incidents built from behaviour-rule findings that are attributed to an agent run. One card per incident kind per run. A rule listed here that cannot fire on a host is reported as such by the catalogue coverage; the card never implies it was watched.

incidents.name: Container Escape
rules: Container Access to Host Sensitive Paths
why: A coding agent has no need to change namespaces, mount devices, load kernel modules or write a cgroup release agent.
Each of these is a known step for leaving a container or sandbox and acting on the host.
actions: Stop the agent and the container it ran in.
Check the host for new files, mounts, kernel modules and processes started after the time shown.
Rebuild the container from a known image rather than reusing it.

incidents.name: Command & Control
rules: Redirect STDOUT/STDIN to Network Connection in Container
Netcat Remote Code Execution in Container
Netcat/Socat Remote Code Execution on Host
why: A shell wired to a network connection lets whoever is on the other end run commands as this user.
Running a program from memory or /dev/shm is how a payload avoids leaving a file on disk.
actions: Stop the agent and any shell or network tool it started.
Look at the Network tab for the address the shell was connected to, and block it.
Treat anything the user could reach as exposed from the time shown.

incidents.name: Persistence
why: A scheduled job, a changed shell start-up file or a new SSH key keeps working after the agent stops.
These are the usual ways to come back to a machine without asking again.
actions: Check crontab, your shell start-up files and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys for entries you did not add, and remove them.
Stop the agent until you know why it made the change.

incidents.name: Privilege Escalation
rules: Potential Local Privilege Escalation via Environment Variables Misuse
why: Setting a setuid bit, abusing sudo or polkit, or attaching to another process are ways to act as root or as another program.
An agent that gains root can read and change anything on the machine.
actions: Look for new setuid files and remove any you did not create: find / -perm -4000 -newer /etc/hostname 2>/dev/null
Patch sudo and polkit if the rule names a known vulnerability.

incidents.name: Log Tampering
why: Clearing logs or shell history removes the record a person would use to see what was done.
It is rarely needed for coding work, and often follows something else worth hiding.
actions: Look at the other incidents and findings for this agent around the same time.
Keep Topgent's own event log: it is kept separately and was not touched by this.

incidents.name: Cryptomining
rules: Detect outbound connections to common miner pool ports
Detect crypto miners using the Stratum protocol
why: A miner uses this machine's power for someone else's benefit.
It usually arrives through a compromised package or a prompt-injected agent.
actions: Stop the agent and the miner process.
Check what the agent installed or downloaded before the time shown.

incidents.name: Credential Access
why: Keys, tokens and passwords are what someone needs to act as you elsewhere.
A coding task rarely needs to search for them or read another program's secrets.
actions: Check the Files tab for this agent: what it read and where its data went afterwards.
Rotate any credential named here if the agent also sent data out.

limits: This is based on behaviour rules that matched the agent's system calls. Topgent saw the calls, not the intent behind them.
A rule that cannot fire on this host is listed under Coverage. Behaviour it covers is not reported here.
